Introduction
AI chatbots have become a primary tool for information retrieval,
with 62.8% of the internet users citing information retrieval as a top
reason for going online [10]. In WebArena, VisualWebArena, and
WebVoyager [16, 20, 47]) platforms, chatbots read the page content,
autonomously execute actions (e.g., clicking buttons and links or
filling out forms), and return answers in a chat sidebar. Yet despite
this capability, a fundamental problem remains: These autonomous
agents return answers without referencing where they are
extracted from, and act without pausing for user verification.
Users must blindly trust every automated step and manually cross-
check answers against a webpage—making it challenging to inspect,
correct, or intervene (see Figure 1a).
Commercial LLM assistants (e.g., RealWebAssist [43], Browser-
Use [7], ChatGPT Atlas [30], Dia Browser [36]) and browser-integrated
agents (e.g., Claude in Chrome [4], Gemini in Chrome [12], OpenAI
Operator [31]) optimize for en-to-end web navigation but make no
attempt to ground their outputs in the page or expose intermediate
decisions to the user. Grounded reasoning approaches such as HoT
[29] and ScreenAI [5] link model outputs to evidence spans, but
do so within the model’s response text—the webpage itself is left
unchanged, so users still have to locate the evidence themselves.
Standard keyword search (e.g., Ctrl+F) is limited to exact string
matching and cannot answer questions or highlight supporting
evidence in context. Content filtering tools such as ad blockers
[15] rely on fixed CSS rules and cannot adapt to a user’s semantic
intent. None of these approaches give users a way to verify answers,
confirm actions, or semantically hide unwanted content—all on the
page.
Three specific user needs remain unaddressed. (1) Finding and
verifying information on dense, cluttered pages is tedious: users
must scan long pages manually to find where AI answers may
be generated based on [46]. (2) Completing multi-step tasks
with step-level oversight is risky without step-level oversight
[8, 19, 21, 24, 27, 37, 41, 44]: users often need to follow many steps
(e.g., clicking, scrolling, navigating menus) to complete tasks such
as changing a password. However, chatbot instructions are long
and do not point to where each step should be performed on the
page, making them hard to follow. (3) Staying focused amid
distracting content is increasingly difficult. While 1 in 3 of the
internet users already use ad blockers [15] and prior work shows
distraction reduction improves task performance [13, 23], users still
lack control over what they want to hide. For example, users may
want to temporarily hide political posts during election periods so
they can focus on essential tasks and reduce exposure to distracting
or emotionally charged content [25, 33]. However, existing tools
rely on fixed rules that cannot adapt to users’ specific goals or to
novel webpage layouts [18].
We present PageGuide, a browser extension that addresses
all three needs by grounding LLM answers directly in the HTML
DOM (e.g., a specific paragraph, button, or link on the page) via
visual overlays. PageGuide offers three main features: (1) Find
links model answers to specific HTML DOM elements via inline
citations, highlighting supporting evidence in-place so users can
instantly verify any claim without leaving the page (Figure 1b);
(2) Guide shows step-by-step instructions to perform a task, one
step at a time, with each target element highlighted on the page
and the user confirming each step before proceeding—following
the mixed-initiative copilot model [2, 17, 34, 41] (Figure 2); and
(3) Hide interprets a natural-language hide request, scores HTML
DOM elements against the user’s intent, and presents a review-
able checklist before hiding the elements, each with a per-element
justification (Figure 3).
To evaluate PageGuide, we conduct a within-subject controlled
user study (𝑁=94) on websites (Section 3.7), where each participant
completed 6 tasks (2 per mode) under both a control condition
(standard browser tools) and an extension condition, with order-
ing counterbalanced to mitigate learning effects. We measure task
completion time, accuracy, behavioral signals (Ctrl+F usage, page
visits), and post-task Likert ratings. Our study aims to answer three
central research questions:
RQ1: Does PageGuide improve task completion accuracy and suc-
cess rate across all three features?
RQ2: Does PageGuide reduce task completion time and interaction
effort (e.g., Ctrl+F usage, mouse clicks, page visits) across Find,
Guide, and Hide tasks?
RQ3: Do users perceive completing tasks with PageGuide as easier
and less effortful compared to completing the same tasks without it?
By systematically comparing between two conditions (control
and extension), we aim to provide rigorous empirical evidence
on whether grounding LLM outputs in the HTML DOM leads to
measurable improvements in task efficiency, accuracy, and user
experience across all three interaction features.
In summary, this paper makes three contributions:
(1) A unified Find–Guide–Hide framework that grounds LLM an-
swers in the HTML DOM, prioritizing in-situ inspectability
over opaque end-to-end automation.
(2) A controlled user study (𝑁=94) and benchmark evaluation
demonstrating that grounded, verifiable web interaction

2
Related Work
Web agents are built to serve a purpose: helping users accomplish
goals on the web more efficiently and accurately than they could
alone. Yet the dominant design paradigm (i.e., fully autonomous
agents that plan, click, and return a final result) conflates com-
pleting a task with serving the user. When a user needs to ver-
ify a claim on a cluttered page, follow a multi-step task, or stay
focused amid irrelevant content, end-to-end automation offers
little help. Prior work can be understood through two orthog-
onal design choices that determine how well a system actually
serves users in these situations: (i) autonomy level, whether the
system acts on behalf of the user or alongside them; and (ii) out-
put grounding, whether the answer is returned without showing
where it comes from on the page or linked to specific, visible ele-
ments. Systems that score high on autonomy and low on grounding
(most existing agents) maximize speed at the cost of verifiability.
PageGuide inverts this trade-off: it acts as a copilot that grounds
every output (e.g., answers, guidance steps, and hiding decisions)
directly in the HTML DOM, keeping the user in control at every
stage.
Web Agents and Browser Automation. LLM-based web agents
have made rapid progress on benchmarks that measure end-to-
end task success [11, 16, 20, 47]. Early systems such as Auto-GPT
[32] and BabyAGI [28] decompose high-level goals into sub-tasks,
execute them via code or tool calls, and iterate until done. More re-
cently, browser-integrated systems—OpenAI Operator [31], Claude
in Chrome [3], Gemini in Chrome [12], Browser Use [7], Dia Browser
[36], and ChatGPT Atlas [30]—embed LLM planners directly in the
browser, enabling click, type, scroll, and navigate actions on pages.
All of these systems sit at the high-autonomy, low-grounding end
of the design space: they handle the task for the user and return a
final result, but their intermediate decisions are opaque and they
do not show where the output comes from on the page.

This opacity carries real costs. Recent benchmarks show that au-
tonomous web agents often make incorrect decisions in high-stakes
situations—such as deleting data, making unintended purchases,
or following deceptive “Download” buttons that expose personal
information [8, 21, 24, 37, 44]. A partial remedy is the copilot model
named Cowpilot [41], where the agent proposes actions and the
user is able to pause, reject, or take alternative action when needed.
PageGuide extends this idea further by not only requesting confir-
mation but grounding each proposed action in the specific HTML
DOM element it will affect, hinting what will happen next, so users
can verify intent before execution rather than trusting an opaque
plan.
Chain-of-Thought and Grounded Reasoning. Chain-of-Thought
(CoT) prompting improves LLM accuracy by externalizing interme-
diate reasoning steps [1, 26, 35, 39]. Highlighted Chain-of-Thought
(HoT) [29] takes this further by embedding XML-style evidence tags
in each reasoning step, linking conclusions to specific input spans
so users can trace why an answer is produced. Vision-language
work on web interfaces reinforces this direction: ScreenAI [5] and
WebQuest [38] show that reliable web interaction requires aligning
model outputs with screen elements and multimodal page evidence,
not just fluent text.
These approaches share a common limitation: evidence is sur-
faced in the model’s output—a sidebar answer, a tagged span, a
cited region—while the webpage in the browser stays exactly as it
is. The user sees the model point to evidence but must scroll back
to the page and locate it themselves. PageGuide closes this gap
by moving evidence directly onto the page: instead of returning
“the answer is supported by element 42,” it places a highlight on
element 42 in the HTML DOM, making the evidence visible exactly
where the user is already looking. This shifts grounding from a
feature of the model’s text output into a live, interactive layer on
the webpage itself—one that users can inspect, override, and act on
without switching context.
Content Moderation and Selective Filtering. Existing filtering
tools operate at the rule level: Ad blockers [15] match URLs and CSS
selectors, Purpose-Mode [23] simplifiers hide predefined element
classes, and task-focused readers strip non-content regions [13, 15,
23]. These rules are static, require manual updates as page layouts
change, and cannot respond to a user’s natural-language intent (e.g.,
“hide posts that feel politically divisive”). Research on personalized
moderation confirms that users want more agency over what gets
filtered and clearer explanations for why [18], yet current tools offer
neither: they hide content silently, with no per-element justification
and no way for the user to review or override individual decisions.
PageGuide’s Hide mode approaches this problem through the
output grounding len: rather than applying a fixed rule, it interprets
the user’s intent at query time, scores each HTML DOM element
against that intent using an LLM, and surfaces a one-sentence
hiding reason for every hidden element directly on the page. The
user can inspect each decision, restore individual elements, and
re-run filtering as new content loads in infinite-scroll feeds. This
turns content hiding from an opaque background process into a
transparent, user-steered interaction.

where agent and user can work together.

Method
3.1
System Overview
PageGuide is a Manifest v3 Chrome extension that injects content
scripts into webpages, giving it both read and write access to the
HTML DOM in real time. As shown in Figure 4, the system follows
a three-step pipeline: the Router classifies the user’s query and
dispatches it to the appropriate handler; each handler reads the
HTML DOM to ground its answers in the current page state; and
the handler produces a final state by mutating the HTML DOM
directly, highlighting evidence, surfacing step-by-step instructions,
or hiding distracting elements. The three handlers differ in how
they interact with the user after the initial HTML DOM read:
• Find is single-pass: the agent identifies supporting evidence
spans and renders inline highlights on the page in one shot.
• Guide is iterative: the agent proposes one action at a time,
the user confirms or skips it (the Feedback loop in Figure 4,
and the agent re-reads the HTML DOM on the new page
before generating the next step.
• Hide is single-pass: the agent scores all HTML DOM ele-
ments against the user’s hiding intent and applies

Across all three features, every text output is coupled to a HTML
DOM mutation: Find returns a text answer with clickable inline
citations that scroll to and highlight the source element on the
page; Guide outputs predicted actions alongside a visual highlight
on the target element; and Hide hides matched elements in place
with an attached reason. The page itself is always the primary
output surface. To ensure that these cross-component interactions
function correctly in a browser (e.g., MS Edge, Chrome), we main-
tain a comprehensive end-to-end testing framework built on Play-
wright, and integrate it with automated continuous integration (CI)
via GitHub Actions. (see Appendix I).

must convert the HTML DOM into a form the LLM can work with.
Using a Set-of-Marks (SoM) [20] style approach, every visible, text-

3.4
Find Mode: Grounded Information
Retrieval
Find addresses a core limitation of existing LLM-based web agents:
answers that are fluent but unverifiable because there is no pointer
on the screen for users to follow or locate information. Given query
𝑞and element index D, Find prompts the LLM (see the full prompt
in Figure 14 in Appendix) to produce a natural language answer
in which every factual claim is annotated with an inline citation
[N:"exact phrase"] , where N is the SoM index of the supporting
HTML DOM element and exact phrase is the precise text span
to highlight. For example, a Find answer for “Who directed this
movie?” might read: “The movie was directed by [45:"Nolan"] and
produced by [12:"Emma"] .”
PageGuide then resolves each citation: it locates the HTML DOM
node at index N, wraps the matching text span in a color-coded
animated overlay (colors are drawn from a luminance-aware palette
so highlights remain distinguishable against any page background),
and scrolls the viewport to the first cited element. The final state
visible to the user has two coupled components (see Figure 1b):
• In-page highlights: each cited span is highlighted directly
on the page; clicking a highlight re-scrolls and re-pulses the
element.
• Side panel answer: the full answer with all citations ren-
dered as clickable anchors is shown in a collapsible panel
alongside the page.
This keeps evidence in situ: the user verifies a claim by glancing
at the highlighted element on the same page rather than switching
context.

3.6
Hide Mode: Transparent Content Hiding
Hide enables users to hide irrelevant or distracting content using
a natural language description (e.g., “hide all sponsored posts”; see
Figure 3). Unlike static ad-blockers that match fixed CSS selectors
or URL patterns, Hide uses LLM to identify elements that the users
want to hide, adapting to novel page layouts and semantically-
specified criteria.

to hide, each paired with a one-sentence justification and a short

Each row in the dialog displays a numbered badge, the hiding
reason in purple, the content snippet, and a a jump button (

Every row is checked by default; the user can uncheck any item

3.7
Data Collection
To evaluate how well PageGuide assists users in finding correct
information, guiding them through realistic web tasks, and hiding
specific webpage content, we construct the PageGuide dataset,
which consists of three subsets: Find, Guide, and Hide. For details
on how each dataset is constructed, please refer to Appendix F.
Find Subset. For Find subset, we randomly sample 5 questions
from Google Natural Questions [22], which provides questions and
answers grounded in webpage content. However, this source alone
is not sufficient for the user study, as many examples are centered
on Wikipedia-style pages with relatively short content, making
the answers easy to find. To better evaluate the efficiency of the
Find feature in diverse, long, and content-heavy webpage settings,
we augment the task set with 5 additional FIND tasks from other
websites.
Guide Subset. The goal of the Guide dataset is to examine how
well PageGuide assists users in completing web-based tasks through
step-by-step guidance. This requires tasks that reflect real user
needs and require a certain degree of human supervision (refer
to Figure 2). Existing datasets, such as Mind2Web [11], Online-
Mind2Web [42], and WebArena [47], are primarily designed to
evaluate autonomous web agents rather than to examine
how an agent assists a human user in completing a task. As a
result, some tasks are less appropriate for a user study since they
are not well aligned with assistive guidance. We therefore construct
a Guide subset consisting of 138 tasks spanning 37 websites. From
this larger task pool, we select 7 representative tasks for the user
study.
Hide Subset. The objective of the Hide dataset is to study whether
PageGuide can hide specific webpage elements in response to a
user’s request. This requires tasks that pair a hide request with the
exact webpage elements that should be concealed. To the best of
our knowledge, existing benchmarks do not capture this specific
problem. We therefore introduce a dedicated Hide subset consisting
of 108 tasks, including 67 easy, 22 medium, and 19 hard instances.
We define task difficulty based on the number of target item types
specified in the user request: easy tasks involve hiding a single type
of target (e.g., “Hide all advertisements on the page”), medium tasks
involve two types (e.g., “Hide all posts that relate to Microsoft or
Amazon”), and hard tasks involve three or more (e.g., “Hide all food
items that contain pineapple, pepper and ginger”). We then select
10 Hide tasks for the user study. We also evaluate the agent’s per-
formance on the full Hide dataset to provide broader quantitative
context for our user-study results (see Appendix D).

4.2
Quantitative Results
Next, we present experimental results from our user study and
address the three research questions introduced in Section 1.
RQ1) Step-by-Step Guidance Increases Task Completion Ac-
curacy For Find tasks, participant accuracy increases from 81% in
the control condition to 86% (+5 pp) with PageGuide as shown in
Figure 5. This improvement is consistent with the system’s design:
by grounding answers directly in highlighted evidence, users are
able to verify information in context rather than relying on memory
or manual scanning. However, a paired Student’s t-test shows that
this improvement is not statistically significant (𝑡= −1, 𝑝= 0.32),
suggesting a modest effect size. This means that while PageGuide
provides a consistent accuracy gain, the effect size for Find
tasks is relatively modest. We attribute this to the already high
baseline performance of Find tasks, which leaves limited room for
further gains.
For Hide tasks, performance is evaluated using accuracy, as the
goal is to correctly identify all relevant elements to hide. Accuracy
improves substantially from 30% in the control condition to 56%
(+26 pp) with PageGuide, as shown in Figure 5. This difference is
statistically significant (𝑡= −4.4, 𝑝< 10−5), indicating a large per-
formance gain. This result reflects the benefit of PageGuide
in helping users more reliably identify all relevant elements
compared to manual inspection.
For Guide tasks, evaluation is more challenging due to their
interactive and open-ended nature. We manually evaluate task cor-
rectness by inspecting each participant’s final screenshot. Only
23% of participants in the control condition successfully reach the
correct terminal state, compared to 53% (+30 pp) with PageGuide,
as shown in Figure 5. This difference is statistically significant
(𝑡= −5.1, 𝑝< 10−8), representing a large improvement. This result
highlights the difficulty of multi-step procedural tasks without assis-
tance, and demonstrates that step-level guidance of PageGuide
with highlighted targets substantially increases users’ ability
to reach the correct outcome.

5
Limitations and Future Work
Single-mode dispatch limits composite tasks. The current in-
tent router maps each query to exactly one mode, which works
well for clearly scoped requests but fails on composite queries that
span multiple features, e.g., “find the settings page and guide me
through changing my password” requires both a Find and a Guide
step. Future work will replace the single-mode router with a multi-
step planner that decomposes composite queries into an ordered
sequence of mode invocations (e.g., Find →Guide), handling tasks
that currently require users to issue multiple separate queries.
Evidence highlights lack cross-page persistence. Find’s in-
page highlights occasionally overwhelmed participants on dense
pages with many matching spans. Additionally, the current imple-
mentation highlights only within a single page; users who navigate
across multiple pages to gather information must re-issue the query
each time. Future work will introduce a re-ranking step that surfaces
the most relevant evidence first, and explore multi-page context:
persisting and aggregating highlights across page visits so users
can build up a cross-page evidence trail within a single session.
Per-step confirmation in GUIDE may introduce overhead When
task time is measured only over correctly completed tasks, PageGuide
is consistently faster than the control condition in the GUIDE tasks
(Figure 6). The remaining limitation is that the per-step confirma-
tion model adds overhead for users who already know the pro-
cedure. Future work will explore adaptive step granularity that
compresses self-evident actions into a single confirmation, and
multi-turn correction (e.g., “skip this step”, “undo the last action”) so
experienced users can move at their own pace.
Content hiding has no memory across sessions. Hide’s confir-
mation dialog added review overhead that some participants found
cumbersome for long lists of matched elements. More broadly, users
currently have no memory across sessions: content they routinely
hide must be re-specified each time. Future work will introduce
a user preference history that persists hiding decisions across
sessions—learning what a user dislikes over time and applying those
preferences automatically on revisited pages, with the ability to
review and edit the saved profile.
6
Conclusion
We presented PageGuide, a browser extension that grounds LLM
answers directly in the HTML DOM across three interaction fea-
tures: Find locates and highlights supporting evidence in-place
so users can instantly verify answers; Guide delivers step-by-step
instructions one action at a time with user confirmation at each
step; and Hide hides distracting content with a per-element justifi-
cation shown in a pre-action review dialog. In all three features, the
agent’s output is embedded in the page itself rather than returned
as plain text in a sidebar.
A controlled user study (𝑁=94) against unaided browsing showed
consistent gains across all features. Find reduced task time by 15.2%
and Ctrl+F usage from 24.1% to 4.4% of tasks, with page visits drop-
ping by 44.3%. Guide improved navigation completion by 7.7%
while keeping users in full control of every action. Hide reduced
task time by 50.8% and improved content hiding accuracy by 25.7%,
enabling users to identify targeted elements they would otherwise
overlook.
These results support the core thesis of this work: grounded, in-
situ interaction—where every answer, step, and hiding decision is
anchored to a specific HTML DOM element—is more effective than
opaque autonomy for tasks where users need to understand why an
answer is correct, how a procedure should unfold, or what has been

D.1
Intent Router Reliably Classifies User
Intent
The intent router is the first and most critical component in PageGuide
(in Section 3): a misrouted query sends the user’s request to the
wrong execution mode, causing failures regardless of how well
Find, Guide, or Hide perform individually. Before evaluating each
mode in isolation, we therefore need to establish that the router
operates with high reliability across all three task categories.
Experiment We constructed a labeled evaluation set of 1,208 nat-
ural language queries covering three routing classes: find (find-
ing information, 969 queries), guide (step-by-step guidance, 132
queries), and hide (hiding content, 107 queries). Queries for the find
class were drawn from the Natural Questions and QASPER datasets
[9, 22], guide queries from the Online-Mind2Web benchmark [11],
and hide queries from a custom dataset collected across 100 diverse
websites (see Section 3.7). We report per-class accuracy and error
type to identify systematic failure modes.
Results The intent router achieves a highly reliable 97.68% overall
accuracy, confirming that it provides a robust gateway for down-
stream execution (Table 1). It correctly classifies all guide queries
(100%) and maintains high accuracy across both the find (97.4%) and
hide (97.2%) classes. The 25 errors in the find class are entirely mis-
routed to guide, a misclassification that can arise from ambiguous
phrasing (e.g., “find me a...”) where information retrieval overlaps
with navigation intent. Lastly, the hide class errors consist of three
queries misclassified as find, which typically occurs when an am-
biguous query that do not convey the hide intent clearly (e.g., “I
only want courses that have higher than 4.6 star.”).

Data Generation Pipeline
We construct the dataset through three separate pipelines for Find,
Guide and Hide subsets. (refer to Figure 17).
Find Subset To construct the Find subset, we collect webpages on
the internet and examples from existing resources, such as Google
Natural Questions Dataset[22]. We then filter for long, content-
dense pages in which the answer is present but not immediately
obvious, requiring users to locate specific information within sub-
stantial page content. From these pages, we extract requests and
manually validate the resulting examples before exporting the fi-
nal dataset. In total, the Find subset contains 10 questions (see
Figure 17A).
Guide Subset The construction of Guide subset follows a four
stage pipeline: collect webpages, select official documentations, ex-
tract guide requests and export dataset. (refer to Figure 17b). Firstly,
we select popular websites based on global web traffic rankings,
using the list of most-visited websites compiled from Similarweb
and Semrush [40]. We then collect official documentation, help-
center articles, and tutorial pages associated with these websites
on different common user-facing tasks (e.g., changing a setting, ap-
plying a filter, or navigating to a feature.) Next, we extract requests
from the help pages and, in some cases, rewrite these procedures
into an actual user requests. Finally, we perform manual quality
control to remove outdated, ambiguous, or duplicate tasks. The
resulting Guide examples each contain a natural-language request,
the reference length and the corresponding website link.

Beyond Basic Functionality: Enhancing Web
Extensions with PDF Reading, Visual
Question Answering, and Page-Off Support
PageGuide extends beyond the core Find, Hide, and Guide func-
tionalities with three additional features: PDF reading, visual ques-
tion answering, and Page-Off support. These features are motivated
by an important limitation of conventional web extensions: user
needs are often not confined to the visible content of the current
webpage. In practice, users frequently interact with documents such
as PDFs, compare webpage content with uploaded images, or ask
questions that go beyond the active tab. Supporting these settings
allows PageGuide to provide a more complete and flexible brows-
ing experience, rather than restricting assistance to page-bound
interactions alone.
PDF Reading Many webpages contain or link to information in
PDF form, such as papers, reports, manuals, and forms. However,
this content is often difficult to browse efficiently using standard
web tools. The PDF reading feature allows users to upload a PDF
and ask questions about its content, enabling the agent to support
document-centered information seeking within the same interac-
tion framework as webpage assistance (Figure 18).
Visual Question Asking Users also often need to reason about
visual content in addition to text. For example, they may want
to compare an uploaded object with items shown on a webpage,
identify whether two images depict the same kind of object, or
retrieve page information relevant to a visual query. The visual
question asking feature allows users to upload an image and ask
questions about it. The agent answers by grounding its textual
response and visual highlights of the uploaded image in the textual
content of the webpage, thereby extending webpage assistance to
multimodal interactions (Figure 19).
Page-Off Feature Not all user questions are tied to the current
webpage. In realistic browsing sessions, users may ask follow-up
questions, seek related background information, or shift to a new
intent while remaining in the extension interface. The Page-Off
feature supports such free-form questions that are not directly
related to the active page, allowing the extension to remain useful
even when the user’s information need moves beyond the current
tab (Figure 20).

End-to-End Testing Framework
PageGuide employs Playwright as its end-to-end (E2E) testing
framework, integrated into an automated continuous integration
(CI) pipeline using GitHub Actions. This pipeline is triggered on
each push and pull request to the main branch, invoking npm run
ci to execute manifest validation, unit tests, and the full Playwright
browser suite in sequence. The rationale for E2E testing stems from
the inherent limitations of unit testing in the context of browser
extension development: numerous failure modes appear only when
code executes within a real Chromium environment, where it must
interact with native browser APIs, extension-specific permissions,
and live page contexts. Accordingly, E2E tests are designed to de-
tect integration-level defects that unit tests cannot surface, includ-
ing extension initialization failures, content-script injection errors,
UI regressions, and cross-component interactions among the side
panel, options page, and background service worker.
The Playwright configuration instantiates Chromium with a
persistent browser context, enabling the unpacked extension to be
loaded via the –load-extension and –disable-extensions-except
launch flags. Test coverage encompasses extension loading and ini-
tialization, service worker and background script startup, side panel
rendering and user interaction, options page functionality, and PDF
viewer integration. Additional edge cases are also tested, including
pages with minimal content, extended scrollable layouts, and image-
dense documents. Collectively, this framework provides empirical
validation that PageGuide operates correctly as a fully integrated
browser extension, rather than relying solely on the correctness of
individual, isolated modules.
